title: RCC RefCert: A Research Toolkit for Structure-Fair Quantum Circuit Complexity
description:
RCC RefCert is an open-source toolkit for studying quantum circuit complexity. Given the parameters of your preparation model, you can compute a rigorous lower bound on optimal quantum circuit complexity from final-state data. Use the target state's exact spectrum or projector counts collected under a prespecified measurement protocol.

You can build your own quantum models and compare preparation strategies. With a density matrix, you can study how complexity is distributed across the subsystems of a pure or mixed state. Share the model, inputs and results for independent verification.

The toolkit is based on Reference-Contingent Complexity (RCC), introduced by Liu, Tian and Wu in Structure-Fair Quantum Circuit Complexity: An Auditable Information-Theoretic Lower Bound. The paper also discusses how RCC's lower bound on the cost of preparing a boundary state relates to holographic complexity (CV/CA).

Features of reference-contingent complexity

Structural fairness makes circuit complexity comparable across physical settings

Quantum circuit complexity is often measured by the minimum number of gates needed to prepare a target state from a fixed initial state. Counting starts once the inputs are ready, so equal gate counts can conceal different physical costs. For example, one device may supply a pure ancillary qubit, while another must first reset a qubit in a mixed state to obtain one. RCC treats structural fairness as a physical postulate, taking the structure reliably supplied by the physical background as the reference zero point. It counts only the resources used to generate additional structure. With these resources measured on a common scale, quantum circuit complexity can be compared across preparation settings.

Final-state data give a rigorous lower bound on optimal circuit complexity

With the model, cost rules and required accuracy fixed, optimal quantum circuit complexity is the infimum of the costs of all circuits that successfully prepare the target. Each such circuit must generate the structure the target requires beyond what the reference already supplies. Even when this global optimum is hard to compute directly, RCC can turn final-state data alone into an auditable certificate that establishes a rigorous lower bound.

Research tasks

  • Build a finite-control model for RCC certification. Describe your setup in terms of its reference state, available quantum channels and control rules. Once you verify its reference bound, you can use that bound for different targets in the same model.
  • Certify a lower bound on optimal circuit complexity. Rule out circuits below the certified cost for the specified target and tolerance. Use an exact target spectrum or fixed-projector measurement counts at a prespecified confidence level. The worked example goes from a model certificate to a cost bound.
  • Compare preparation strategies. See which programs reach your target within tolerance and what each one costs. For exact diagonal-preserving models, the cyclic-reset and algorithmic-cooling examples show when the bounds establish the optimum and when a gap remains.
  • Analyze pure-state complexity with window RCC. Compare pure states with the same global RCC value to see how their complexity is distributed across subsystems. The same window analysis applies to mixed states. With your own density matrices, you can separate local and correlation contributions and track how each changes during preparation.
  • Share a calculation for independent verification. Send a colleague one bundle containing the original inputs and results so they can recompute and verify the calculation independently.
  • Reproduce the paper's reference calculations. Run python -m rcc_refcert reproduce --check to reproduce the bundled cases. Three MATCH results confirm agreement with the frozen expectations, data and report. The paper-to-code map connects the cases to the paper's equations.

Run and share a calculation

With Python 3.10 or newer, install version 0.3.0 and run the four-qubit reset task in a new working directory.

python -m pip install "rcc-refcert==0.3.0"
python -m rcc_refcert cost template cyclic-reset > task.json
python -m rcc_refcert cost analyze task.json --bundle task.rccbundle

At the default trace-distance tolerance of 1/10, the result is [5,5] atomic slots. The model rules out shorter programs, and a five-slot program reaches the target with halt included. Change epsilon in task.json to try another tolerance and choose a new bundle filename for the next run. Verify the saved calculation with the following command.

python -m rcc_refcert bundle verify task.rccbundle

Version 0.3.0 adds preparation-cost intervals and subsystem complexity profiles. Both workflows support independent recomputation from a saved bundle.

Interpreting the results

Exact diagonal-preserving models can bracket the optimal preparation cost between a rigorous lower bound and the cost of a successful program. For general matrix models, the numerical checks give each candidate's cost and trace distance from the target. Window RCC compares state-side complexity at a fixed reference and control bandwidth. A finite-accuracy lower bound on preparation cost also uses the model parameters and one-shot corrections. The scientific scope explains the quantities and their units.

Further reading

The RCC paper also relates these bounds to the complexity–volume and complexity–action conjectures in high-energy physics when the preparation task and resource conventions are aligned.
